extracted.intended_audience: patent drafters, patent attorneys, and inventors preparing patent applications
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for drafting and organizing patent claims (independent and dependent), selecting claim formats and fallback positions, and adapting claim sets across jurisdictions (EPO, PCT, USPTO).

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent versus dependent claims (definition and determination)
rubrics_metrics.description: An independent claim is a claim that does not depend from any other previous claim; a dependent claim depends from another claim when it makes an explicit reference to that claim and its scope is a subset of the base claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether a claim is dependent from another depends on both the claimed subject matters and whether a reference is made from one claim to another. Examples: Claim 1 independent; Claim 2 dependent from Claim 1; Claim 3 dependent from Claim 2 (and, logically, also dependent from Claim 1 because its scope is a subset).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim dependency groups and chains (identify and analyze)
rubrics_metrics.description: Separate claim sets into dependency groups (each formed of a single independent claim and all claims depending from it) and analyze each group or chain separately for validity and infringement assessments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start by separating out different dependency groups or chains. Consider each group independently when assessing novelty, inventive step, and infringement (illustrated by Figures 4–8).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependency pyramid risk and fallback position planning
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid creating a dependency pyramid where many dependent claims all ultimately depend only from a single broad independent claim (the pyramid vertex), because this gives poor fallback positions if the independent claim is invalidated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When EPO-style multiple dependencies are converted improperly (e.g., changed to all depend on Claim 1), a dependency pyramid may be created — not generally recommended. Plan dependent claims as fallback positions in case independent claim lacks novelty or inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drafting independent claim to state essential elements
rubrics_metrics.description: The independent claim should state the essential elements of the invention — the elements necessary to achieve the technical effect underlying the solution of the technical problem — and these elements should be explicitly described in the description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include all essential elements required for essential functionality. To achieve broad protection, stretch essential elements to their greatest reasonable extent, taking into account essential functionality and prior art. Do not draft as a 'mere desideratum' (state result without saying how achieved). For product claims, define the elements/technical features that give rise to an effect, not the effect itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use dependent claims as fallback positions
rubrics_metrics.description: Draft dependent claims to cover more particular embodiments and to act as fallback positions should the independent claim be found not novel or lack inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify order of importance of elements during brainstorming and draft dependent claims accordingly. In general, draft one dependent claim per selected/added element. Dependent claims can add selected values or further characterize elements. Consider business and enforcement strategy when ordering dependent claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple dependent versus singular dependent forms (jurisdictional practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple dependent claims (claims that depend from multiple preceding claims) are permitted in some jurisdictions (e.g., EPO) but are not allowed at the USPTO; choose appropriate dependency forms for the target office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write multiple dependent form for EPO when adding extra elements is desirable. Before entering the US national phase, deconstruct multiple dependencies into singular dependencies by preparing chains with broadest, narrowest and intermediate meanings. Consider claim count limits/fees (EPO allows fewer free claims than some offices; USPTO has limits and amendment/added-matter issues).

rubrics_metrics.name: Converting EPO multiple dependencies to USPTO-style claims
rubrics_metrics.description: When adapting claims drafted in EPO style (including multiple dependencies) to USPTO practice, prepare singular dependency chains representing broadest and narrowest meanings and possibly intermediate claims to stay within practical claim counts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare (i) dependency chains with broadest meanings of elements, (ii) chains with narrowest meanings, and (iii) intermediate claims if needed. Aim to keep total claims reasonably limited (ideally no more than ~20 to avoid extra fees). Provide clear instructions if drafting is transferred to another drafter to avoid accidental creation of a dependency pyramid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markush groups and alternative elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Markush groups to claim an element as being selected from a group of alternatives (e.g., 'element D being D1, D2 or D3') to capture alternatives within claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Markush groups can broaden claim scope and allow later dependent claims to pick specific alternatives (e.g., Claims 4–6 selecting D1, D2, D3). A dependent claim that adds an element selected from a group can only depend on preceding claims that provide antecedent basis for that element.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choosing claim format (standard format vs two-part format)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether to draft the independent claim in standard (single-part) or two-part format; EPO examiners may request two-part format where distinguishing from prior art is desirable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two-part format separates known features (preamble) from the characterizing portion. Example: where prior art discloses 'a writing device having A11 and B11', two-part format could read 'A writing device comprising: element A; and element B; characterized by further comprising element C...'. Choose format with awareness of prior art and office practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preamble with purposive 'for' expression (functional limitation caution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that include a preamble with a purposive expression (e.g., 'An apparatus for carrying out the process ...') may be construed in many jurisdictions as covering an apparatus merely suitable for that purpose, which can affect novelty and infringement scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious using 'for' wording — it can imply suitability rather than a functional limitation. e.g., an apparatus claimed 'for molten steel' may exclude items unsuitable for molten steel. Distinguish cases where the purpose is a true functional feature of a method claim versus where it denotes mere suitability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty assessment using dependency analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess novelty by comparing claim scopes (starting with the independent claim) against prior art; novelty of an independent claim implies novelty of dependent claims in that chain with respect to that prior art reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a prior art reference falls outside the independent claim, then by definition it falls outside all dependent claims in that chain (simplifying validity assessment). Be careful not to assume that invalidity of an independent claim necessarily implies invalidity of all dependent claims (a common nonexpert mistake). Also novel does not equal valid — inventive step must also be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literal infringement assessment using dependency analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine literal infringement by comparing the accused embodiment with claim scopes; if the accused embodiment falls inside the scope of a dependent claim, it may also fall within the scope of its base claims, but infringement conclusions must be drawn carefully by chain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A finding that the accused embodiment falls outside an independent claim simplifies infringement assessment (none in that dependency chain will be infringed). Conversely, if it falls within a dependent claim, the dependent's base claim elements may also be present — but do not assume infringement of an independent claim implies infringement of all dependents nor vice versa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draft concisely: remove unnecessary words while preserving essence
rubrics_metrics.description: Once the essence of the invention is captured, review claims to remove as many words as possible while still preserving the invention's essence, involving inventors as needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Professional tip: re-review claims for unnecessary adjectives/words (e.g., 'pivotal' in a mounting may be unnecessary). Concision can broaden scope and reduce inadvertent limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product (apparatus) claim drafting principles
rubrics_metrics.description: When drafting a product/apparatus claim, prepare a preamble reciting what the apparatus is (and sometimes what it does) and list essential elements required for the invention to function in its basic form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In general, infringement of a product claim occurs when third parties make, use, offer for sale, sell or import the product. Ensure essential components that confer novelty are captured in the claim body.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process (method) claim drafting principles
rubrics_metrics.description: A process claim should list the series of steps performed; in many jurisdictions steps are presumed to occur in any order unless the claim specifies order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about ordering when order matters. For infringement, unauthorized use of claimed process infringes; products directly obtained by a claimed process may also be encompassed (depending on jurisdiction). Consider whether steps like adding milk/sugar are essential to the claimed invention or removable to broaden scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use claims and jurisdictional treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims to use of a product in a process (use claims) are treated differently by jurisdictions: EPO treats a use claim as equivalent to a process claim phrased as a process for doing X, while the US generally requires a process claim form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft use claims mindful of target jurisdictions; in some offices you must draft as a process claim to be acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-by-process claims: limits and evidentiary burden
rubrics_metrics.description: Product-by-process claims (product defined by its process of manufacture) are allowable in some jurisdictions but the claimed product still must satisfy novelty and inventive step; the applicant bears the burden to show that the product so obtained is different if challenged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some offices (EPO) treat the claim as a claim to the product as such and extend protection to products directly obtained; in Japan product-by-process claims may be considered indefinite and used only in special circumstances. Provide evidence that process parameters produce a different product when relying on such claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parameter claims (claims defined by measurable values)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims may define inventions by characteristic measurable parameters (e.g., melting point, viscosity) where the invention cannot otherwise be defined without undue restriction and where the result is directly verifiable by tests specified in the description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the specification includes adequate directions to enable verification by routine tests. Parameter claims are useful when structural definition is impracticable but must be supported by the description so the skilled person can determine values without undue experimentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antecedent basis for dependent claims
rubrics_metrics.description: A dependent claim that adds an element selected from a group or further characterizes an element can depend only from preceding claims that provide an antecedent for that element; a dependent claim adding an extra element (not a selection) does not need antecedent and can depend from any preceding claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When drafting dependent claims, ensure antecedent basis is proper (the element referenced must have been introduced earlier). For selected elements (e.g., a value chosen from a Markush group), dependency must be to claims that provide that antecedent.
